summary: Discovery call focused on Redwood reliability options: Odyssey is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for low-latency customer-facing inference. Main concerns: multi-region failover, SLA guarantees, cache consistency during region failover, and data residency/KMS requirements. Redwood AE+SE walked through routing/fallbacks, dedicated capacity, and options for private VPC deployments. Agreed to run benchmarks and share pricing/SOC2 docs.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-01-11 15:00 PT | Duration 52m | Attendees: Maya, Ravi (Redwood); Lena, Marcus, Priya (Odyssey)

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro - i'm maya redwood AE, ravi's our solutions eng. how are you all
[00:05] Lena Ortiz: good, thanks. we'll keep it focused - want to understand reliability story and what happens during region outages
[00:12] Ravi Patel: sure, happy to. maybe to set context, can you share your current infra and where the ssn of traffic is coming from?
[00:20] Marcus Huang: yeah - we're mostly on GCP us-central1 for API traffic, some eu traffic via a CDN. main product is real-time scoring for ad relevance, P95 latency target is <120ms and p99 under 300ms.
[00:35] Priya Singh: also we have strict data residency for some EU customers; if we need private deployment we need VPC peering + KMS integration.
[00:45] Ravi Patel: got it. so main concerns are latency, routing, and also how you survive an incident in a region - like multi-region fallback and cache behavior during failover?
[00:55] Lena Ortiz: exactly. we've seen incidents where cache warmup causes a big spike in latency. how does redwood handle prefix cache and kv cache when routing between regions or model variants?
[01:05] Ravi Patel: great question. in hosted mode we do automatic routing by policy - latency first or cost-first - and we have model variants that are compatible for fallback. KV cache is per-region by default, so we use a prefix-based cache hop to keep warm entries for hot prefixes, but there is a cold-start window on region failover. you can mitigate by pre-warming, or using a shared cache in dedicated/private via a managed redis if needed. note: some transcribed names might be off - we call it KV cache internally.
[01:30] Marcus Huang: managed redis, interesting. but for us the bigger ask is predictable SLA - we need to know if we can route traffic to another region and keep SLA for customers.
[01:40] Maya Chen: on dedicated we provide reserved capacity with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets. for multi-region we support active-active routing or active-passive with health checks; routing can failover to a secondary region automatically with policy you set.
[01:55] Priya Singh: during failover, do you guarantee model parity? we have concerns about model version skew or quantization differences causing inference drift.
[02:03] Ravi Patel: yes - good callout. we recommend pinning model versions across regions; our rollout system ensures consistent model artifacts. for quantized variants we mark compatibility and do automatic conversion paths, but you should test quality/regression with your eval prompts.
[02:18] Lena Ortiz: what about cost - if we route to dedicated in another region temporarily, are we billed for both regions or just usage?
[02:25] Maya Chen: billing depends on deployment. for reserved dedicated capacity you'd have committed monthly costs per pool; we can enable burst capacity in a secondary region billed on usage. we'll share pricing details but the baseline is reserved plus usage for bursts.
[02:40] Marcus Huang: okay. security questions: SSO, audit logs, kms - does private deployment support HSM-backed keys?
[02:48] Ravi Patel: Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integration, and audit logs are delivered to your project. SAML SSO and RBAC are supported in the control plane. SOC2 report and ISO snippets we can share.
[03:02] Priya Singh: in an outage scenario, how do you route if the control plane is in redwood hosted region? does private deployment give us a separate control plane?
[03:10] Maya Chen: for Private we offer a customer-controlled control plane option - that can sit in your VPC or on-prem. for hosted/dedicated, control plane is multi-region and we have failover mechanisms; still we often recommend Private for strict no-external-control-plane requirements.
[03:28] Lena Ortiz: any customers running active-active multi-region with redwood?
[03:32] Ravi Patel: yes - a few analytics customers do active-active with traffic steering at the edge. common pattern is edge load balancer -> region-local redwood endpoints -> consistent model versions. they do periodic cache replication or pre-warm jobs to reduce cold-starts after failover.
[03:50] Marcus Huang: can we do per-tenant routing so EU traffic never leaves eu? that's mandatory for a subset of our clients.
[03:58] Maya Chen: absolutely - routing policies support geo-routing and per-tenant rules; you can pin tenants to dedicated pools in eu-west while others hit us-central.
[04:08] Priya Singh: when a region goes down, how do you handle in-flight requests and queued jobs?
[04:15] Ravi Patel: in-flight requests are retried by the client LB; we also offer client-side SDKs with idempotency tokens for safe retries. queued work in a region will either drain if you set a graceful drain window or be redirected to a fallback region depending on your policy.
transcript_continued:
[04:40] Marcus Huang: curious about the SLA math - do you provide a latency SLA or only uptime?
[04:45] Maya Chen: for dedicated we provide both uptime and latency SLOs at the pool level; example p95 latency SLOs can be part of the contract. In hosted we publish performance profiles but it's not SLA-backed for all tiers.
[05:00] Lena Ortiz: what about testing - can we run a simulated region outage test?
[05:05] Ravi Patel: yes, we can run a chaos test in your staging: bring down a region, measure failover time, and show cache-warm behavior. we'll set up a benchmark harness with your traffic patterns.
[05:18] Priya Singh: do you have RBAC separation for ops vs engineering? we need audit trails for who changed routing or rollouts.
[05:24] Maya Chen: RBAC is granular, role-based access is supported; audits are available and integrated to SIEM via log forwarders.
[05:32] Marcus Huang: any limitations on model size or seq length across regions during failover?
[05:36] Ravi Patel: model size limits are per-inference runtime instance - if you have very large models we recommend dedicated pools and same instance types across regions to ensure parity. sequence length is configurable but pricing/latency vary.
[05:48] Lena Ortiz: walk me through a realistic timeline if we want private deployment with VPC peering - how long?
[05:55] Maya Chen: private VPC setup is typically 6-8 weeks depending on network approvals and KMS setup; on-prem can be longer for air-gapped. Dedicated reserved pools can be provisioned faster, usually 2-3 weeks.
[06:10] Priya Singh: ok - let's talk follow ups.
[06:12] Maya Chen: recap: we will run a 48hr benchmark using your sample traffic, we'll share Dedicated pricing and SOC2 docs, and schedule a technical deep dive to cover cache replication and chaos testing.
[06:24] Lena Ortiz: sounds good. one last quick question - what happens to rate limits when you failover? do you preserve quotas?
[06:31] Ravi Patel: rate limits are per-tenant and can be global or region-scoped depending on your config; during failover we can preserve quotas by routing through a global quota service or allow temporary overage with throttling based on policy.
[06:44] Marcus Huang: good to know. thanks everyone.
[06:47] Maya Chen: thanks - we'll follow up with docs.

End of transcript.
